prayer.text: Saint Ignatius of Antioch, pray for us.

cues.text: Bishop of Antioch
Ignatius, surnamed Theophorus — the God-bearer — was born in Syria about the middle of the first century.
Ancient tradition, supported by the strongly Johannine cast of his thought, counts him a disciple of the Apostle St. John , together with his friend Polycarp .
He became the third Bishop of Antioch , the great city where the disciples were first called Christians, following (if Peter is counted) the Apostle himself and Evodius.
For decades he shepherded that church in a time of danger.
Condemned to the Beasts
Under the emperor Trajan Ignatius was arrested and condemned to be thrown to the wild beasts in the arena at Rome.
He was placed under a guard of ten soldiers, whom he wryly called ten leopards , and taken the long way across Asia Minor to the capital.
Far from dreading his fate, he longed for it as the consummation of his discipleship, and begged the Christians of Rome to do nothing to deprive him of it.
The Seven Letters
On that journey Ignatius wrote the seven letters that have made him one of the most precious voices of the sub-apostolic age.
From Smyrna and then from Troas he sent letters to the churches of Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia, and Smyrna, and one to Polycarp , bishop of Smyrna.
Written by a man walking knowingly to his death, they burn with love for Christ and concern for the unity and orthodoxy of the churches he would never see again.
Witness to the Church
The letters are a cornerstone of the Church's early self-understanding.

Ignatius is among the earliest surviving writers to describe clearly the threefold ministry of bishop, priests, and deacons as essential to the Church's unity, urging the faithful to do nothing without the bishop.
And in his letter to the Smyrnaeans he uses one of the earliest surviving instances of the expression "the Catholic Church".
Witness to the Eucharist
With equal clarity Ignatius witnesses to the Real Presence.
He calls the Eucharist the medicine of immortality, the antidote that we should not die, and warns against those who abstain from it because they will not confess that it is the very flesh of Christ.
For Ignatius the visible unity of the Church around her bishop and her altar is inseparable from the truth of the Incarnation itself.
A Voice from the Sub-Apostolic Age
Because Ignatius wrote within a generation of the Apostles, and wrote knowing death was near, his letters carry a weight that few documents of the early Church possess.

They reveal a Christianity already ordered and sacramental, gathered around bishop, altar, and creed, and already naming itself Catholic — not a later structure imposed on a formless beginning, but the visible shape of the faith from the first.
For this reason, his seven epistles have been cited in every age as evidence of what Christians believed while the memory of the Apostles was still fresh.
They remain a favourite witness in the Church's understanding of her own origins.
Martyrdom in Rome
Reaching Rome about the year 107, Ignatius was given to the beasts in the amphitheatre, and his longing was fulfilled.
In the most famous of all his words he had written ahead to the Roman Christians that he was the wheat of God, to be ground by the teeth of the beasts into the pure bread of Christ.
His feast is kept on October 17 .
With Clement of Rome and Polycarp he is numbered among the Apostolic Fathers, early Christian leaders who preserved and handed on the faith received from the apostolic age.
